title: Norilsk: thawing ground and the TPP-3 tank collapse

sections.headline: Was the ground under Norilsk sinking, and did that bring down tank 5?
sections.text: On 29 May 2020 fuel tank no. 5 of the TPP-3 power plant collapsed and ~21,000 t of diesel reached the Ambarnaya river. One study (Zhang et al. 2022) blamed thawing permafrost; the federal inspectorate (Rostekhnadzor, Nov 2020) blamed the pile foundation. We measured ground motion with radar satellites 2017-2026.

sections.headline: Wetlands sink every summer, as thawing ground should, and the rate is not growing
sections.text: Compared with their ~2 km surroundings, herbaceous wetlands sink every summer in proportion to the square root of accumulated thaw (Stefan's law), with the same coefficient in all six summers 2017-2025: no sign of acceleration. The same places sink every summer, and NISAR (L-band, 2026) sees it independently.

key_numbers.label: Same pattern in two summers: r

sections.caveats: Motion of the whole lowland relative to bedrock is not measurable (atmosphere). Part of the wetland signal could be water-level effects on the radar.

sections.headline: Industrial ground does not sink more than other lowland ground
sections.text: Industrial zones behave like random lowland ground, and plants such as TPP-3 do not sink more than their surroundings in any summer.

key_numbers.label: Sites that 'sink every summer' vs chance

sections.headline: No ground subsidence under tank 5 in the thaw seasons; a small, local settlement in its last winter
sections.text: Relative to the structures around it, tank 5 did not sink in the snow-free summers 2017-2019, when thawing ground would settle; the steady -35 mm/yr of Zhang et al. 2022 is not seen. In its last winter (Dec 2019 - Apr 2020), while the ground was frozen, tank 5 alone settled about 1.5 cm relative to its surroundings, step by step from January; none of 20 other tanks and tank-row structures did, including the one 117 m away. The result survives every check we could run (unwrapping, median, weighting, height error, leaving out any single image). It fits a failing foundation; it is strong evidence of movement, not proof of its cause.

sections.caveats: Dry snow delays the radar (~1 mm per mm of snow water): a drift at the tank could mimic settlement, although the steps do not follow blowing-snow episodes and the neighbouring tank did not move; tanks elsewhere show ~1 cm excursions in other periods (snow onset, autumn 2019). One track, one sensor, 20 m pixels (no tilt); whole-tank motion cannot be compared with damage thresholds, which refer to differences within one tank.

sections.headline: The bedrock under Norilsk is not sinking
sections.text: The GNSS station NRIL, on bedrock in Norilsk, rises slightly. A regional subsidence like the -30.8 mm/yr area mean of Zhang et al. 2022 does not exist in the bedrock; our InSAR reference (plateau bedrock) is a sound zero.

sections.headline: Foundation failure, not ground thaw
sections.text: The radar shows no thaw-driven settlement of the ground at the tank or the plant before the collapse, and no regional subsidence of the bedrock. This agrees with the inspectorate's finding: pile cap and piles too weak (33 piles failed in a chain, ~30% not on rock), tank returned to service in 2019 without notifying the regulator, no permafrost degradation found. Permafrost thaw is real in Norilsk - wetlands sink every summer - but it is not what the data show at tank 5. Warming of the frozen ground around the piles cannot be ruled out.

sections.headline: What this cannot say
sections.text: No radar data over Norilsk in 2022-2024; motion of the lowland relative to bedrock is atmosphere-dominated; C-band loses the signal at snowmelt and snow onset, so winter and summer cannot be linked; settlement within one tank (tilt) is below the 20 m resolution; uniform settlement of a whole area is invisible to the relative measures used here.
